findings.title: Blocked email lookup is case-sensitive, so a block is trivially bypassed
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact-match lookup: BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first. On PostgreSQL string equality is case-sensitive, and nothing normalizes case anywhere in the flow: User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] exactly as typed, BlockedEmail.set_defaults only sets action_type, and EmailValidator passes the raw value through. An admin who blocks spammer@example.com will not block Spammer@example.com or SPAMMER@example.com, even though those deliver to the same mailbox, so a blocked spammer can re-register simply by changing letter case. Normalize the address (e.g. strip + downcase) both when writing blocked_emails rows and when checking in should_block?, or query with a case-insensitive comparison such as lower(email) = lower(?). The added specs only exercise exact-case matches, so this gap is not covered by tests.

findings.title: match_count is incremented per validation pass, so one signup attempt is counted twice
findings.body: should_block? has a database write side effect (match_count += 1 and save) and is invoked from EmailValidator, meaning it runs every time a User is validated. UsersController#create validates the user twice per attempt: once explicitly in `if user.valid? && SiteSetting.call_discourse_hub?` (users_controller.rb line 168) and again inside `user.save` (line 172). Because the record is new and unsaved, email_changed? is true for both passes, so a single blocked signup attempt increments match_count by 2 and updates last_match_at twice. Any other code that calls user.valid? and then user.save (or calls valid? as a dry-run check) also mutates these statistics. Match tracking should live outside the validation cycle (e.g. in the controller after a failed save) or otherwise be per-attempt rather than per-validation, otherwise the match_count/last_match_at audit data this feature exists to collect is unreliable.

findings.title: match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write
findings.body: should_block? does record.match_count += 1 followed by record.save. That is a read-modify-write: two concurrent requests matching the same blocked email can both read the same counter value, and one increment is silently lost. If these statistics are meant to be accurate, use an atomic update such as BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_counters(match_count: 1) plus an update of last_match_at, instead of incrementing an in-memory attribute and saving the whole record.
